blocks.text: **Devmaxx topic:** Consistency. **Goal:** choose a consistency model per operation and defend it with a business reason.
Consistency is not a system-wide setting. It is **a decision per operation** (or per data class).

rows: Money must not be duplicated or lost
A follower count off by 3 for 2 seconds is fine

blocks.text: **The interview question that reveals seniority:** "Which of these *specifically* needs strong consistency, and why? What breaks if it's eventually consistent?" Answering "everything needs to be consistent" is the mark of a junior.
CAP (Gilbert & Lynch)
When a **network partition** occurs, a distributed system must choose between:

items.text: **C — Consistency**: every read returns the most recent write (linearizable)
**A — Availability**: every request to a non-failing node returns a response (not necessarily

blocks.text: the latest)

items.text: **P — Partition tolerance**: the system continues to operate despite arbitrary message loss

blocks.text: **The real statement:** *when a partition happens, you must choose C or A.* You can't have all three (and P isn't optional in a distributed system — partitions always happen).
The common misreading
"CAP says pick 2 of 3" — **false and very widely repeated.**

Actually: P is mandatory. During a partition you choose **C** (CP system — refuse requests / block until healed, e.g. Postgres primary-replica, ZooKeeper, etcd, HBase) or **A** (AP system — serve stale data and reconcile later, e.g. Cassandra, DynamoDB, Riak).
PACELC (a better model)

Most real systems are **PC/AC** (Postgres-like) or **PA/EL** (Dynamo-like). This adds the crucial insight that **even without a partition, you trade consistency for latency** — that's the trade you make on every request, and CAP only describes the partition case.
What this means in practice

items.text: **CP systems** (Postgres, MongoDB with majority write concern, ZooKeeper, etcd, HBase, Spanner,

blocks.text: CockroachDB): during a partition, one side of the partition **rejects writes** (or reads) rather than serving stale data. Availability is sacrificed for correctness.

items.text: **AP systems** (Cassandra, DynamoDB, Riak, CouchDB): during a partition, **both sides accept

blocks.text: writes** and reconcile later. Availability is preserved, consistency is eventual.

items.text: **PACELC is not "eventual consistency is fine"** — it says the trade is *latency vs consistency

blocks.text: on every request*, and *availability vs consistency only during a partition*.

sections.title: 3. Consistency models, from strongest to weakest

rows: All operations appear to happen at a single instant, in real-time order
Coordination on every op; may block or fail during partitions
All operations appear in a consistent order, but not necessarily real-time order
Causally related operations are seen in order; concurrent ops may be reordered
You always see your own writes
You never see a value go backwards
If writes stop, all replicas converge eventually (no guarantee of *when*)

blocks.text: Linearizability
The practical test: **is there a total order of operations consistent with real time, and does every read return the latest write in that order?**
Practically: a linearizable read must go to a node that knows about the latest write — the primary, or a replica that has applied it and can prove it (via a lease or a quorum read).

**Lease-based linearizability**: a read takes a lease from a quorum (majority) with a short expiry, guaranteeing no concurrent write can also hold a lease. This is how Spanner and many "strongly consistent KV" systems work. The cost is one quorum round trip per read/write.

sections.title: 4. Quorums: the math you must know

blocks.text: For **R** replicas, write to **W**, read from **R_quorum**:

blocks.code:
W + R > N     →  the read and write quorums overlap
             →  the reader must see the latest write
             →  strong-ish consistency

items.text: Write succeeds when ≥2 replicas ack → at most 1 replica is stale.
Read of 2 replicas → at least one is up to date. ✓

blocks.text: **Example (N = 3, W = 1, R = 3):** 1 + 3 > 3 ✓ — but a write only needed one replica, so it may still be in flight; the read will catch it eventually but you pay full read cost.
**Example (N = 3, W = 2, R = 1):** 2 + 1 = 3, not > 3 → **a read can miss the write entirely**. This is the classic misconfiguration.
Latency and availability of quorums

blocks.code: Availability of a quorum operation = P(all required replicas reachable)

blocks.text: With N=3, W=2: if each replica is 99.9% available and independent, quorum availability ≈ 1 - (0.1% * 0.1% * 3) ≈ 99.99997%. High. But if replicas share an AZ and that AZ fails, quorum availability collapses. **Place replicas across failure domains**, and remember that cross-AZ RTT (1–2 ms) is the price of quorum reads.
Dynamo-style "R, W, and the read repair"
Dynamo's N=3, W=2, R=2 default gives "eventual-ish" but overlapping-quorum reads. Real Dynamo adds:

items.text: **Read repair**: a read that returns stale values triggers a background write to fix them.
**Sloppy quorum**: if fewer than W replicas are available, write to a temporary "hinted" node

blocks.text: (in Dynamo) — improves availability at the cost of extra reconciliation work.

sections.title: 5. CAP in practice: choosing the store

rows: Linearizable; used for coordination, not user data

sections.title: 6. Update propagation: how changes actually flow

blocks.text: Synchronous vs. asynchronous cascade

blocks.code: Client → Service → Store A (write) → [async] → Store B (derived index)

blocks.text: The gap between A and B is the **inconsistency window**. Design questions:

items.text: How long is it acceptable?
How is it detected when it exceeds the bound?
Who repairs it?

blocks.text: Change data capture (CDC)
A log of every change, streamed to consumers:

items.text: Postgres logical replication / Debezium → Kafka.
DynamoDB Streams, Kinesis.
**Benefits**: derived indexes, caches, search, analytics, audit logs, and **outbox relay** all

blocks.text: consume the same stream.

items.text: **Challenge**: exactly-once is hard; consumers must be **idempotent** (Ch. 08).

blocks.text: Dual writes and their failure mode

blocks.code:
db.write(order)          # succeeds
kafka.send(order_event)  # fails  ← order saved but event never published

blocks.text: **Fix: transactional outbox.** Write the business row and an outbox row in one local DB transaction. A relay reads the outbox and publishes to Kafka (retries, dedups by event ID). The invariant becomes "the event is published **at least once**", and consumers are idempotent.
This is one of the most valuable patterns in this entire curriculum. Learn it cold.
In any at-least-once system, **the same operation will happen more than once**. Design for it.
Idempotency keys
Server behavior:

items.text: Look up the key. If a completed result exists, **return it** (same status code, same body).
If in progress, return 409 or wait.
Otherwise, execute, store `key → response` atomically with the effect, and return.

blocks.text: Implementation in Postgres:
Insert the key with `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`; if 0 rows inserted, someone else is processing it.
Natural idempotency
Some operations are inherently idempotent: `SET x = 5` (not `x = x + 5`), `DELETE` (not `INCREMENT`), upserts, `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE`.
**Prefer naturally idempotent operations.** "Set status to 'shipped'" is idempotent; "increment counter" is not.
Deduplication windows
For streams, keep a set of recently-seen event IDs (Redis SET with TTL, or a DB table) and skip duplicates.
2PC in detail

blocks.code:
Coordinator → Participants: PREPARE
Participants: write to a "prepared" state, reply PREPARED or ABORT
Coordinator → Participants: COMMIT (if all PREPARED) or ABORT

blocks.text: **The problems:**

items.text: **Blocking**: if the coordinator dies after some participants prepared, participants hold locks

blocks.text: and wait forever. Recovery requires a coordinator recovery procedure.

items.text: **Performance**: 2 extra round trips on the write path.
**SPOF**: the coordinator is a single point of failure (mitigated by replicated coordinators).

blocks.text: **Do not use 2PC across services in a microservices architecture.** Use sagas or outbox.
Sagas in detail
A saga is a sequence of local transactions, each with a compensating action:

blocks.code:
T1: Reserve inventory   → C1: Release inventory
T2: Charge payment      → C2: Refund payment
T3: Create shipment     → C3: Cancel shipment

blocks.text: **Saga rules:**

items.text: Each step must be **idempotent** (compensations may run multiple times).
Each step's compensation must be **commutative/independent**.
You need **no isolation** between steps — intermediate states are visible. Design the UX for it

blocks.text: ("Payment pending, confirming shipment…").

items.text: Use a **saga orchestrator** (a state machine that knows the steps) rather than pure choreography

blocks.text: (event-based) when the flow has branches or compensations; choreography gets hard to reason about beyond ~4 steps.

items.text: Persist saga state durably so it can resume after a crash.

blocks.text: Last-write-wins (LWW)
Compare timestamps (or a hybrid logical clock). Simple, but:

items.text: Clock skew causes a **later** write on a node with a fast clock to lose.
Loses concurrent updates silently.

blocks.text: Hybrid Logical Clocks (HLC)
A timestamp combining physical time with a logical counter, guaranteed monotonic per node. Popular (CockroachDB) because it's compact and preserves causality better than wall-clock.
Vector clocks
Per-node counters: `{"A": 3, "B": 1}`. Compare to detect **causal** relationships:

items.text: `A > B` → A's event is causally after B's → no conflict, A wins.
Concurrent → real conflict → resolve by application logic (merge, ask the user, keep both).

blocks.text: Cost: metadata grows with the number of nodes.
CRDTs
Data structures designed so concurrent updates **always converge** without coordination:

items.text: **G-Counter** (grow-only counter), **PN-Counter** (additive)
**LWW-Register**
**OR-Set** (observed-remove set) — for like/unlike
**RGA / Logoot** — for ordered sequences (text editing)
**Delta-state CRDTs**, **AVRM** (add-wins map)

blocks.text: Use CRDTs when you need offline-first, multi-region writes, or collaborative editing, and you can accept the data-model constraints.
When designing an operation that *must* be linearizable, verify:

items.text: **Where does the write go?** The primary/leader — a single authoritative node.
**How does the read know?** Either read from the primary, or read from replicas with a quorum that includes the primary's latest write, or use a lease.

**What if the primary fails mid-write?** The write is either durable (committed & replicated) or not; failover picks the replica with the highest applied LSN. Partial writes are rolled back or completed; the client gets an error or a retry, and the retry is idempotent.

**What if the client times out?** It doesn't know if the write committed. **This is the hardest case.** Answer: the client must retry with an idempotency key, and the server must be able to tell "already done" from "not done". Never rely on the client knowing.
**What if two clients write concurrently to the same key?** Serialization via the primary's ordering; the last write wins *at the primary* (that's fine — that's linearizable).
**What's the failover RPO?** If the write was acked but not replicated, failover loses it → the ack was a lie. This is why sync/semi-sync replication matters for critical writes.

**Implement a quorum KV store.** In-memory, N nodes, `put(key, value, W)` and `get(key, R)`. Simulate: a node going down, a network partition, and concurrent writes. Verify: (a) `W + R > N` yields no stale reads; (b) `W + R <= N` **does** yield stale reads (find the case).
**Implement LWW vs. vector clocks.** Two nodes, concurrent writes to the same key. Show LWW losing a write due to clock skew; show vector clocks detecting the conflict.

**Transactional outbox, end to end.** A service writes to Postgres; an outbox relay publishes to a queue; a consumer processes and updates a derived "read model" table. Kill the relay mid-flight, restart it, and verify no events are lost and no duplicates cause double-processing (idempotency key on the consumer).
**Saga with compensation.** Implement: reserve inventory → charge payment → create shipment. Inject failures at each step and verify the compensations restore the initial state.

blocks.text: Good: "For the balance I'll use linearizable reads and writes against the primary — money can't be stale. For the feed, eventual consistency is fine; I'll serve from a materialized view that's a few seconds behind, and I'll use the outbox pattern so the feed updates reliably."

Better: "The tricky part is the read-after-write on the profile page. If the read hits a replica that hasn't caught up, the user sees their old name. I'll return a commit token from the write and route the read to a replica that's caught up, falling back to the primary."
Red flags: "CAP means pick 2 of 3"; "we'll use eventual consistency everywhere"; "2PC across services"; no mention of idempotency for at-least-once delivery.

selfCheck.q: **State CAP correctly. Why is "pick 2 of 3" a misreading?**
selfCheck.a: When a network partition occurs, you must choose **C** (reject/block to preserve consistency) or **A** (serve possibly-stale data). Partition tolerance isn't optional — partitions always happen — so the real choice is C-vs-A during a partition, not "pick two."

It adds the **else** branch: when there's *no* partition, you still trade consistency for latency on every request (PACELC: PA/EL). This captures the everyday cost of strong consistency (extra round trips) that CAP's partition-only framing hides.

selfCheck.q: **N=3, W=2, R=2. Prove that a read never returns a stale value.**
selfCheck.a: A write is acked only after ≥2 of 3 replicas store it. So at most 1 replica lacks it. A read of 2 replicas can only miss the write if *both* it reads lack it — but at most 1 can lack it. So the read must include a replica that has the write. ✓

selfCheck.q: **N=3, W=2, R=1. Show a stale read is possible.**
selfCheck.a: The write is stored on replicas A and B. Replica C lacks it. A read of R=1 can hit C and return the old value. 2 + 1 = 3, which is not > N, so the quorums need not overlap. ✗

selfCheck.q: **Give an example of an operation that must be linearizable and one where eventual is fine.**
selfCheck.a: Linearizable: transferring money between accounts (double-spend is unacceptable); placing an order (can't oversell inventory); a seat reservation. Eventual: follower counts, view counters, a trending feed, a search index, "last seen" timestamps.
You write a value, then read it back and get the *old* value — from a lagging replica. Breaks user trust ("I changed my name and it didn't save!").

selfCheck.q: **What is the dual-write problem, and how does the outbox pattern fix it?**
selfCheck.a: Writing to the DB and then publishing to a broker is two independent operations; the first can succeed and the second fail, leaving the DB and the event stream permanently out of sync (and you can't tell which happened). Fix: write the business row and an outbox row in **one local DB transaction**, then have a relay publish outbox rows to the broker with retries. Guarantees "published at least once"; consumers dedupe by event ID.

selfCheck.q: **What does idempotency mean, and why is it required in any at-least-once system?**
selfCheck.a: Idempotency means applying the operation multiple times has the same effect as applying it once. At-least-once delivery guarantees duplicates will happen (network retries, consumer crashes after processing but before acking, relay redelivery). Without idempotency, duplicates cause double charges, double emails, double inventory decrements.

selfCheck.q: **Give a natural idempotent version of `counter = counter + 1`.**
selfCheck.a: `SET counter = 42` (an absolute set) is idempotent. Or `UPSERT` with an absolute value. The increment form is not idempotent: applying it twice gives +2.

2PC blocks (participants hold locks waiting for the coordinator), requires a highly available coordinator, adds round trips to the write path, and couples the availability of unrelated services — during a partition, one unavailable participant stalls the whole transaction. Microservices need local autonomy, so sagas/outbox are used instead.

selfCheck.q: **What is a saga, and what property does it give up compared to 2PC?**
selfCheck.a: A saga is a sequence of local transactions across services, each with a compensating action to undo it. It gives up **atomicity** (there's no all-or-nothing moment; intermediate states are visible) and **isolation** (no snapshot isolation across steps). In exchange it avoids blocking and 2PC's coordinator dependency.

selfCheck.q: **What are the 3 requirements for CRDT convergence?**
selfCheck.a: The merge function must be **commutative** (order doesn't matter), **associative** (grouping doesn't matter), and **idempotent** (applying twice is the same as once). These three properties guarantee all replicas converge to the same value regardless of message order or duplication.

selfCheck.q: **The client times out after sending a write. It doesn't know if it committed. What should it do, and what must the server support?**
selfCheck.a: The client must **retry with an idempotency key**, and the server must support idempotent replay: store `key → response` atomically with the effect, and on a repeat, return the stored response instead of re-executing. The client must never assume "no response = not committed."

selfCheck.q: **What is a "dirty read" and why do read-committed systems avoid it?**
selfCheck.a: Reading data written by a transaction that later **rolled back**. Read-committed forbids it by only exposing committed rows.

selfCheck.q: **Your write was acknowledged as synchronous but the replica was actually lagging. What went wrong?**
selfCheck.a: Synchronous means the write waits for the replica's ack — but if the ack came from a replica that *later* lost the data (crashed before fsync, disk corruption, or the ack was for a different transaction in a batch), durability was over-promised. This is why real systems need durable storage semantics (`fsync` before ack), replica durability verification, and honest RPO statements — acks mean "committed to N replicas", not "will survive any failure."
